lines.text: Welcome back. Our HTML has created the pieces.
Now we need to decide what those pieces look like.
Same HTML. Same pieces. The only difference between these two... is CSS.
Every CSS rule has two parts.
First, who you're styling. That's the selector.
Then, what you're changing, inside the curly brackets. A property, and a value.
The hash symbol means id. So hash player means, the thing with the id player.
And a dot means class. So dot cloud means, every cloud.
First, we pick our colours, and give them names. These are called variables.
Later, we'll use these names, instead of typing colour codes again and again.
Want a purple dinosaur? Change one line.
This is our design system. Decisions we make once, and use everywhere.
Now the page. We center everything, and switch on our Quicksand font.
max width stops the game getting too wide on big screens.
And the score gets bold.
Now the world appears. Three hundred pixels tall. Sky blue. A border, and rounded corners.
border radius rounds the corners. Small number, slightly round. Big number, very round.
Change the background, and you change the whole environment. Daytime. Sunset. Night.
position relative turns the game area into a map. Anything inside it can be placed exactly.
Then the ground. Forty pixels tall, stuck to the bottom. Those stripes will help us see it move later.
And here's our player.
Position absolute. Sixty pixels from the left. Fifty from the bottom. Forty four wide. Fifty two tall. Orange.
Change the width, and the object changes size.
Change the position, and the object moves.
Hold on to that idea. In video four, JavaScript will change the bottom value sixty times a second. And that's how jumping works.
Before and after let us add extra shapes, without new HTML. One is the eye. The other is a leg.
And a crashed style. When the dino has a class called crashed, it turns red.
Same idea for the cactus. A rounded green rectangle. Plus two arms.
Your paper design might have a rock, a puddle, or a fence. You now know enough to build it.
Now the clouds. Keyframes describe an animation. From here, to there.
We tell each cloud to drift across the sky, forever.
So CSS can animate things. But notice. The clouds don't care what you do. They can't react to a key press.
That's behaviour. And behaviour needs JavaScript.
Next, the messages and the button. Our button gets a pill shape, and a little lift when you hover.
Now let's hide the Game Over box. Display, none.
Wait. It's still showing. Why?
Two rules are fighting over display. CSS has a rule for this. An id is more specific than a class, so the id wins.
This is debugging. Something doesn't do what we expected, so we look at why.
Important tells CSS, this one wins. And the Game Over box disappears.
Look at that. Plain structure, to a styled game.
But press Space...
Nothing. CSS controls the appearance. But our game still doesn't have its real behaviour.
It's like a beautiful car, with no engine.
Your challenge. Change the colours to match your paper design.
Next time, we build the engine. JavaScript.
